join_order.notes: Use lineitem_l_orderkey_grouped index. Qualifying orderkeys are in sorted order (from static partitioned scan of orders sorted by o_orderkey), so lineitem access is sequential.

scan.notes: Late materialize o_shippriority — only load for final top-10 results. Saves scanning 60MB during orders scan.

qualifying_orders.notes: CRITICAL: Use two-pass approach to avoid merge phase. Pass 1: count qualifying rows per thread (static partitioning). Compute prefix sums for offsets. Pass 2: write directly into pre-allocated shared array at computed offsets. Orders are sorted by o_orderkey and static partitioning preserves sort order, so the result array is sorted by orderkey. Allocate with malloc (lazy zero-fill via mmap for large allocations) to avoid upfront zero-initialization cost. Late materialize o_shippriority — NOT included in this struct.

aggregation.notes: Revenue accumulated directly into the compact array during lineitem probe. No separate aggregation map needed.

parallelism.orders_scan: Two-pass with static partitioning. Pass 1: each thread counts qualifying rows in its partition. Pass 2: each thread writes qualifying rows to shared array at precomputed offsets. NO per-thread vectors, NO merge/copy phase.
parallelism.lineitem_probe: Static scheduling over qualifying orders (NOT dynamic). Since qualifying orderkeys are sorted and lineitem is sorted by l_orderkey, static scheduling gives each thread a contiguous range of orderkeys, resulting in sequential access to lineitem files within each thread. This works with MADV_SEQUENTIAL for OS prefetching.
parallelism.notes: CRITICAL: Use schedule(static) for lineitem probe to maintain sequential access pattern across lineitem files. Dynamic scheduling would cause random access.

indexes.purpose: O(1) lookup of contiguous lineitem rows per qualifying orderkey

optimization_notes: Category B+C — Algorithm change + Work elimination. Three root causes: (1) MAP_POPULATE pre-faults page tables for ~706MB (including the 458MB lineitem index where only 6% of entries are accessed), costing 33ms — fix: disable MAP_POPULATE for all files, use demand-paging. (2) Lineitem data columns use MADV_RANDOM which disables OS prefetching, yet access is sequential (sorted qualifying orderkeys) — this causes ~200K unnecessary soft page faults, explaining the 36ms unaccounted time in iter_1. Fix: use MADV_SEQUENTIAL for lineitem data columns, MADV_SEQUENTIAL for orders columns, MADV_RANDOM only for the lineitem index. (3) The merge_sort phase copies 84MB from per-thread vectors to a single array (22ms). Fix: two-pass approach — count qualifying rows per thread in pass 1, compute prefix sums, write directly to pre-allocated shared array in pass 2. Additional: late materialize o_shippriority (skip scanning 60MB, only load for top-10 results). Use schedule(static) for lineitem probe to maintain sequential access. Expected savings: data_loading 33ms→~2ms, unaccounted 36ms→~5ms, merge 22ms→0ms, scan 18ms→~14ms.

lineitem_data_columns.notes: Access is sequential after sorting qualifying orderkeys. MADV_SEQUENTIAL enables OS readahead, eliminating ~200K soft page faults that caused 36ms overhead in iter_1. Do NOT use MADV_RANDOM.

lineitem_l_orderkey_grouped_index.notes: Only 6% of entries accessed. No MAP_POPULATE to avoid faulting 458MB of pages.

mmap_strategy.notes: CRITICAL: Do NOT use MAP_POPULATE for any file. On hot runs, pages are in OS page cache. MAP_POPULATE still costs ~33ms to walk page tables and create PTEs for 706MB. Demand-paging with appropriate MADV_* hints is faster.

o_shippriority.when: After top-10 selection. Only 10 lookups needed instead of scanning all 15M rows.
o_shippriority.how: Store row_id (the orders scan loop index) in the qualifying orders struct. After finding top-10, use row_id to look up o_shippriority[row_id].
